meta.title: Rashid-1 Multi-Needle Langmuir Probe: An Engineering Playbook for Lunar Plasma | StarThermaTech
meta.description: Inside the Rashid-1 rover Langmuir probe payload: multi-height photoelectron sheath measurements, compact high-impedance electronics, bias-sweep I-V retrieval, calibration and vacuum validation, and 3D PIC inversion that can be reused for lunar and terrestrial plasma diagnostics.
title: Rashid-1 Multi-Needle Langmuir Probe: An Engineering Playbook for Lunar Plasma
source: Source: Summary of a recent Space Science Reviews article
summary: A recent review dissects the four-needle Langmuir probe flown on the UAE's Rashid-1 lunar rover. It covers the mission goal, probe layout, compact electronics, bias-sweep operations, calibration and vacuum tests, plus 3D PIC-based inversion—forming a reusable template for lunar and lab plasma diagnostics.
hero.alt: Four-needle Langmuir probe layout on the Rashid-1 lunar rover
hero.caption: Rashid-1 mounts four identical probes at different heights while keeping electronics compact and low power.
section1.title: Mission Goal: In-situ Photoelectron Sheath Profiling
section1.p1: The Rashid-1 multi-needle Langmuir probe targets in-situ measurements of electron density, electron temperature, and floating potential during lunar daytime.
section1.p2: By synchronously acquiring I-V curves at multiple heights, the team aimed to resolve the photoelectron-dominated sheath near the regolith and provide an engineering reference for future lunar payloads and ground diagnostics.
section2.title: Probe Layout: Four Heights, Synchronous Views
section2.p1: On an ~11 kg rover, the team integrated four identical needle probes plus a compact electronics board, achieving multi-point measurements under tight mass and power limits.
section2.points.title: Key layout choices
section2.points.item1: Multi-height placement: probes on different rover sides at ~11 / 23 / 38 / 56 cm above ground to span the near-surface vertical profile.
section2.points.item2: Guarded design: coax outer conductor tied to the same bias to suppress support-induced distortion of the I-V curve.
section2.points.item3: Geometric consistency: ~38 mm exposed length, ~1 mm diameter to keep inversion well-conditioned.
section2.points.item4: Surface treatment: graphite coating to lower secondary electron emission and stabilize measurements.
section3.title: Electronics: High-impedance TIA and Dual Gain
section3.p1: All electronics sit on a PC-104 stack inside the rover. Commands arrive via CAN; onboard DACs generate the bias and route it to the selected probe.
section3.p2: To handle extremely tenuous plasma, the TIA uses tens-of-megaohm feedback, giving ~±200 nA range with picoamp-level resolution and 1× / 10× gain modes for dynamic range.
section3.list.title: Signal-chain highlights
section3.list.item1: TIA → differential amp → 16-bit ADC with a low-noise budget end to end.
section3.list.item2: Bias and guard share the same potential to tame edge effects.
section3.list.item3: Commands and telemetry over CAN for low-power, robust control.
section4.title: Operations: Bias Sweep for I-V Retrieval
section4.p1: Nominal mode is a bias sweep: stepping −10 V to +10 V in ~0.1–0.2 V increments, dwelling milliseconds to hundreds of milliseconds per step to capture current and build full I-V curves.
section4.p2: I-V regions (ion saturation, electron retardation, electron saturation) yield electron density, temperature, and plasma potential. Sampling can be tuned from ~60 Hz up to 4 kHz to balance time resolution and data volume.
section4.bullets.title: Processing approach
section4.bullets.item1: Synchronous multi-height sweeps + numerical inversion to recover the sheath-external plasma.
section4.bullets.item2: Configurable sweep parameters to cover daytime and shadow plasma conditions.
section5.title: Calibration & Ground Tests: Quantified Linearity and Noise
section5.p1: Before integration, precision sourcemeter injections of −180 to +180 nA calibrated each channel, yielding linear coefficients and offsets; noise sits at the tens-of-picoamp level.
section5.p2: Thermal-vacuum runs from −25°C to 85°C and argon-plasma chamber tests matched commercial sourcemeter I-V curves, demonstrating reliability in real plasma.
section5.highlights.title: Verification notes
section5.highlights.item1: Temperature drift can be compensated using the enclosure temperature for stable long runs.
section5.highlights.item2: Dual gain keeps usable SNR in both very low and moderate plasma densities.
section5.highlights.item3: Lab comparisons bound system error, giving a baseline for flight data inversion.
section6.title: Modeling and Outcome: Still a Transferable Blueprint
section6.p1: 3D PIC simulations of “solar wind + photoelectrons + regolith + rover + probes” map potential and density, enabling conversion from in-sheath measurements to true ambient density.
section6.p2: The lander carrying Rashid-1 failed during the final descent in 2023, so no lunar data returned, but the chain—from requirements to design, electronics/software, calibration, vacuum testing, and numerical inversion—was proven.
section6.p3: The combo of multi-needle geometry, high-impedance TIAs, bias sweeps, and modeling can be ported directly to vacuum chambers, electric propulsion tests, and low-temperature plasma tools.
footer.note: Compiled from open publications and mission reports as a reference for plasma diagnostics engineering.
